name: Phosphaturic Mesenchymal Tumour
aliases: phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour, mixed connective tissue variant

clinicalPearls: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour is the classic cause of tumour-induced (oncogenic) osteomalacia, a paraneoplastic syndrome driven by tumoural over-secretion of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23).
FGF23 excess causes renal phosphate wasting with hypophosphataemia and inappropriately low or normal active vitamin D, producing osteomalacia in adults or rickets in children.
Typical features are insidious bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, loss of height and recurrent fragility or insufficiency fractures, usually after years of diagnostic delay.
Because phosphate is often absent from routine biochemistry panels, the key clue is missed; a fasting serum phosphate should be checked deliberately.

The distinctive histology is the mixed connective tissue variant (PMTMCT), showing bland spindle cells, flocculent grungy calcification, haemangiopericytoma-like vasculature and osteoclast-like giant cells.
The tumours are typically small, slow-growing and occult, arising anywhere in bone or soft tissue, with acral and craniofacial (sinonasal) sites over-represented.
Somatostatin-receptor functional imaging (for example gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/CT) is the most sensitive means of localising the culprit lesion.
Complete surgical excision is curative with rapid biochemical recovery; recurrent FN1-FGFR1 and, less often, FN1-FGF1 gene fusions have been identified.
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours are rare, usually benign neoplasms of mesenchymal origin that autonomously secrete fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a bone-derived phosphaturic hormone. Circulating FGF23 acts on the renal proximal tubule to downregulate the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporters (NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc), causing renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia, and it simultaneously suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) while inducing 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1), lowering 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and thereby reducing intestinal phosphate absorption. Chronic hypophosphataemia impairs mineralisation of newly formed osteoid, producing osteomalacia. These tumours characteristically harbour recurrent gene fusions, most commonly FN1-FGFR1 and less often FN1-FGF1, which are thought to drive an autocrine or paracrine loop promoting FGF23 production. Because the culprit lesions are frequently tiny and may lie anywhere from the distal extremities to the sinonasal region, and because they express somatostatin receptors, they often remain occult for years until localised by functional imaging.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive hypophosphataemic rickets (DMP1 or ENPP1)
Fanconi syndrome and other proximal renal tubular phosphate-wasting states
Fibrous dysplasia and McCune-Albright syndrome (also FGF23-mediated)
Nutritional osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency, or osteoporosis of other cause
Seronegative spondyloarthropathy or other rheumatological disease mimicking the bone pain and stiffness
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum phosphate with paired assessment of renal phosphate handling (tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate corrected for glomerular filtration rate)
Serum calcium, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone, and 25- and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Intact FGF23 measurement, interpreted as inappropriately elevated for the degree of hypophosphataemia
Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT (for example gallium-68 DOTATATE) to localise the tumour
Cross-sectional MRI or CT of the suspected site to define surgical anatomy
Selective venous sampling for FGF23 when non-invasive imaging is equivocal
Histopathology with immunohistochemistry of the resected lesion to confirm the mixed connective tissue variant
redFlags: Recurrent low-trauma fragility or insufficiency fractures in an adult
Progressive proximal myopathy with a waddling gait and difficulty rising from a chair
Failure of phosphate and active vitamin D supplementation to control symptoms, indicating an unresected tumour
reference.prognosis: The tumours are almost always benign and complete excision is curative, with phosphate and symptoms usually normalising rapidly after surgery. Incompletely resected or persistently occult lesions cause ongoing disease, and rare malignant variants with metastatic potential are recognised.
pitfalls: Because phosphate is not on standard biochemistry panels, the disorder is commonly missed and mislabelled as osteoporosis, fibromyalgia or a rheumatological condition.
FGF23 may fall within the assay reference range yet still be inappropriately high for the degree of hypophosphataemia, so it must be interpreted in context.
Anatomical imaging alone often fails to detect the small tumour; functional somatostatin-receptor imaging is usually required.
Symptoms recurring after apparently successful surgery suggest residual tumour or a second occult lesion rather than a new disease.
references: Endocrinology and metabolic bone reference texts
Bone and soft-tissue tumour pathology references
management: Goal is definitive removal of the FGF23 secreting tumour rather than cytotoxic cancer therapy, since PMT is usually benign and indolent
Complete surgical excision with negative margins is first line and potentially curative once the lesion is localised

For anatomically difficult sites such as skull base or sinonasal locations, image guided minimally invasive surgery or ablative techniques like radiofrequency ablation or cryoablation are alternatives or adjuncts to open surgery
Functional imaging to localise the tumour takes priority over escalating medical therapy, since medical treatment is a bridge and not a cure
Bridging medical therapy with oral phosphate salts plus an active vitamin D agent such as calcitriol corrects hypophosphataemic osteomalacia while surgery is pending or deferred

For inoperable, unresectable, multifocal, or persistently occult disease, an anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody such as burosumab can control hypophosphataemia and may allow reduction of phosphate and vitamin D supplementation
The rare malignant variant or metastatic disease follows the same surgical first principle with multidisciplinary sarcoma type input, since systemic chemotherapy or targeted therapy data are limited
Radiotherapy has no established primary role and systemic chemotherapy is not standard for typical benign PMT
Monitor serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase, and parathyroid hormone regularly to confirm cure after resection or titrate medical therapy in unresected disease
Screen patients on phosphate and active vitamin D therapy periodically for nephrocalcinosis and secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Recurrent or persistent hypophosphataemia after apparent complete resection should prompt repeat functional imaging for residual or a second occult tumour
Refer to endocrinology as soon as tumour-induced osteomalacia is suspected biochemically to guide work-up and functional imaging
Refer to a centre with somatostatin-receptor functional imaging and surgeons experienced in these lesions once localisation is attempted
Refer to a multidisciplinary team including endocrinology, oncology or surgery, radiology, and pathology for unresectable, recurrent, incompletely excised, or malignant disease
